title: India: two hosts, one chain.
summary: Redis module execution opened Delhi; a host-mounted job directory and tar wildcard escaped the container before an SSH agent carried the chain to root on Mumbai.
recon: Delhi exposed SSH and an unauthenticated Redis 6.2 service. Redis reported a working directory inside /data, which matched the containerized layout described in the recovered walkthrough. Mumbai accepted only key-based SSH and was intended to be reached from the first host.
path: A rogue Redis module provided code execution as root inside the Delhi container. The important discovery was not container root; it was /opt/app/data, a host-mounted workflow directory processed by a scheduled archive job. Tar checkpoint filenames and a shell script converted that scheduled job into host execution. The resulting access was used to place an SSH key for the host service account.
escalation: The Delhi service account had access to a live SSH agent. Pointing SSH_AUTH_SOCK at that socket exposed a key accepted by Mumbai. On Mumbai, the admin account could run find through sudo; find's -exec action launched a privileged shell and exposed the proof file.
lessons: Container root is a clue, not a finish line. Enumerate mounts, scheduled consumers, shared directories, and agent sockets. The clean attack graph was Redis RCE → mounted job queue → wildcard execution → Delhi SSH → agent hijack → Mumbai → sudo find.
evidenceNote: Both flags are directly supported by the exported terminal history and by the later competition memory. Flag values and infrastructure details are removed.

title: AD105: three forests.
summary: A workstation foothold became domain compromise through coercion, NTLM relay, RBCD, DCSync, and a final trust/delegation path across three forests.
recon: The environment contained a SOKOLO workstation, two SOKOLO domain controllers, and separate LONIPO and BORITO forests. Initial access was a low-privilege domain user. Local administrator material from the workstation enabled the internal pivot, but it was not domain administrator access.
path: For the first flag, a SOCKS/tunnel path exposed the internal network. PetitPotam coerced a secondary controller to authenticate, and ntlmrelayx forwarded that authentication to LDAPS on a different controller. The relay wrote resource-based constrained delegation, allowing a controlled machine account to impersonate an administrator to the target controller. DCSync then recovered the domain material required to take the controller.
escalation: The remaining work crossed forest boundaries. The export records extensive dead ends around self-relay, SID filtering, and trust direction. The later completion note states that all three flags were obtained: the second through the recovered CVE/trust path and the third through a BloodHound-discovered Kerberos delegation relationship between trusts.
lessons: Draw the domain graph before choosing an exploit. Local admin is not domain admin, self-relay is structurally different from cross-DC relay, and trust direction changes what a ticket can mean. BloodHound was decisive only after the underlying authentication boundaries were understood.
evidenceNote: Flag one has direct command-and-flag evidence. The export later states that all three were solved and names the delegation route for flag three; the final two raw outputs were completed outside the preserved Claude transcript.

title: OpenClaw: reload the model.
summary: A Jupyter foothold, a shared model directory, unsafe pickle loading, and an administrative reload endpoint turned model deployment into code execution.
recon: The target exposed an employee AI environment and a Jupyter service. Recovered notebooks revealed a shared models directory, the internal model-server hostname, and the difference between prediction authentication and the administrative reload API.
path: A crafted pickle was written into the model path shared with the model server. Initial requests proved that deserialization had executed because the health endpoint reported an unexpected model type. The missing piece was not exploitation but lifecycle: the server cached the existing object until its administrative reload route was called with the correct header.
escalation: Reloading the model executed the pickle inside the model-server container. Writing command output back into the shared /models volume made the result visible from Jupyter and completed the lab without requiring a conventional interactive shell.
lessons: In ML infrastructure, trace the artifact lifecycle: where a model is written, mounted, loaded, cached, and reloaded. A deserialization primitive may already be working even when the visible response is only a type error.
evidenceNote: The exploit progression and completion statement survive in the export. Several rich terminal outputs were exported as object placeholders, so this panel reconstructs only the commands supported by adjacent messages.
coverAlt: Close-up of code on a dark computer display

title: NebulaAssist: token to tool.
summary: Prompt injection leaked a protected MCP token in fragments; the hidden server then exposed a debug file-reading tool.
recon: Two Uvicorn services were visible: an employee support portal and an MCP server protected by a bearer token. Registration worked, the chat endpoint streamed responses, and client code documented the token's recognizable mcp_ pattern.
path: Direct requests for the token were redacted. The successful prompt asked for only the portion after the underscore and separated its representation enough to avoid the sanitizer. Reassembling that value authenticated to the second service. MCP initialization and tools/list exposed debug_read_file.
escalation: The debug tool could not read the root proof file but could read the local flag under the service user's home directory. That distinction confirmed both the service identity and the intended one-flag scope.
lessons: Output filtering is not secret isolation. If the model can access a secret, format transformations may turn a blocked exact value into recoverable fragments. Enumerate MCP tools after authentication; debug capabilities often carry more risk than the chat layer.
evidenceNote: The exported history contains the successful MCP session, tools listing, file read, and flag-found confirmation.
coverAlt: Dark code display representing an AI service

title: MCP: the benchmark was a shell.
summary: A model-evaluation tool passed its benchmark argument into a shell command without sanitization.
recon: The service exposed an MCP endpoint alongside an Ollama deployment. After initialization, tools/list returned a model-evaluation function accepting user-controlled evaluation parameters.
path: The benchmark field was treated as data at the protocol layer but interpolated into a command by the implementation. A shell substitution payload proved execution and read the one user-level flag.
escalation: No separate privilege escalation was required. The vulnerable tool already ran with access to the scoped flag.
lessons: Tool schemas describe shape, not safety. Trace every tool argument beyond JSON validation to the subprocess, template, database, or filesystem sink that consumes it.
evidenceNote: The flag-found response and vulnerable parameter name are preserved directly in the export.

title: AutoFlow: the host behind n8n.
summary: An n8n workflow reached a mounted Docker socket; the Docker API then exposed the host filesystem and the root proof.
recon: Nmap identified n8n on 5678. A webhook health path and recovered application credentials opened the workflow UI. Standard fetch-style code failed inside the JavaScript node, so the exploit had to use the runtime's native HTTP module.
path: The workflow environment could reach /run/docker.sock. A JavaScript node spoke HTTP over the Unix socket, created a disposable container with the host root mounted read-only, started it, and collected the container logs.
escalation: Reading the host-mounted /root/proof.txt produced the root flag. The lab was marked complete after that proof because the challenge scope required one flag.
lessons: When a sandboxed workflow lacks fetch, enumerate the runtime rather than abandoning the primitive. A Docker socket is effectively host control; keep the proof action minimal and prefer read-only mounts in a lab.
evidenceNote: The export contains the Docker API output, the root proof path, the flag-found confirmation, and the explicit completion statement.

title: The Leaky Packet.
summary: A supposedly careful exfiltration stream left recoverable data inside repeated DNS queries.
recon: The capture was filtered by protocol and conversation volume. DNS stood out because many requests shared a destination pattern while the changing labels carried unusually structured data.
path: Query labels were exported in packet order, the fixed domain suffix was removed, and the remaining chunks were concatenated and decoded. The reconstructed payload contained the submitted flag.
lessons: For covert-channel forensics, compare what stays fixed with what changes. Entropy, label length, ordering, and retransmissions matter more than the apparent destination name.
evidenceNote: The user explicitly states that Forensics 1 was submitted. The export memory identifies the solved technique as DNS exfiltration.

title: Cache Rules Everything.
summary: Deleted download history did not delete the browser cache objects that recorded the suspect's retrieval.
recon: The supplied profile had cleared download history, so the investigation moved from visible history tables to cache index and data files. URL fragments and response metadata survived independently of the Downloads UI.
path: Searching cache records for URLs, MIME types, and flag-format fragments isolated the downloaded object. Extracting the matching cached response recovered the submitted value.
lessons: Browser deletion features usually target user-facing records, not every cache layer. Treat History, Cache, Code Cache, Service Worker storage, and session artifacts as separate evidence sources.
evidenceNote: The user explicitly states that Forensics 2 was submitted. The challenge name and Chrome-cache source are preserved in the exported request.

title: Russia: Triage AI.
summary: A Flask ticket portal and a FastAPI analysis service formed an AI triage pipeline; the surviving session records deep enumeration but not the team's final proof.
recon: The Moscow host exposed SSH, a Flask/Werkzeug application on 5000, and an internal-looking FastAPI service on 5001. Registration yielded an employee session. Ticket descriptions were queued for AI analysis, while the API expected a session identifier through a specific request shape.
path: The session explored ticket processing, session signing, internal API routing, attachment behavior, and prompt-injection possibilities. It established the two-service architecture but did not preserve a successful exploit or accepted flag.
escalation: No verified escalation survives in this export.
lessons: The useful artifact is the architecture map: authenticated Flask frontend, separate analysis API, asynchronous queue, and server-side session boundary. A future replay should capture every response body and correlate a ticket ID with its analysis session rather than brute-forcing unrelated secrets.
evidenceNote: This is a recovered team dossier, not a claimed solve. It records only steps visible in the export.

title: Australia: DocuFlow.
summary: DocuFlow classified uploaded documents into workflows; the archive records upload, result, and routing behavior but no verified final flag.
recon: The Sydney target hosted DocuFlow on port 5000. The application accepted selected document formats, extracted their text, classified them, and rendered workflow results. Recovered team notes also listed VNC access to competition workstations, which was infrastructure rather than a target vulnerability.
path: The session tested document-type validation, PDF content, classification changes, archive IDs, prompt injection, and possible template rendering. Results such as Standard Archival, Email Forward, and HR Screening were observed. No accepted flag is preserved.
escalation: No verified host escalation survives in the record.
lessons: For AI document pipelines, separate upload parsing, text extraction, model classification, action routing, and template rendering. Each stage has a different input surface; mixing them caused much of the original looping.
evidenceNote: This article is deliberately labeled as a partial reconstruction. It does not invent a solve that the export cannot prove.

title: Morocco: Nexus ServiceHub.
summary: A Koa integration portal exposed a webhook tester whose hostname filter could be bypassed, revealing the internal application on port 3000.
recon: Casablanca exposed SSH and Apache on port 80. The public application was Nexus ServiceHub, a Node/Koa integration platform with notes, integrations, and a webhook test endpoint.
path: Direct localhost requests were blocked, but an sslip.io hostname resolving to the target bypassed the preflight filter. That reached the internal Node service on port 3000 and exposed administrative route behavior, including an internal database-query endpoint. The preserved session ends before a verified flag.
escalation: No verified host-level escalation survives in the export.
lessons: SSRF defenses must validate the resolved address at connection time and after redirects, across IPv4 and IPv6. A hostname allow decision made before resolution is not an internal-network boundary.
evidenceNote: The SSRF bypass and internal routes are directly evidenced; a final solve is not.

title: Argentina: MCP Atlassian.
summary: The team record maps an Atlassian-style frontend, an MCP SSE transport, and an internal file service; the final friend-owned solve transcript was not exported.
recon: Buenos Aires exposed SSH, an Atlassian-themed web frontend on 8080, an MCP server on 9000, and a file service on 5000 reachable from the target context. The MCP transport used an SSE channel plus JSON-RPC messages.
path: Recovered work enumerated MCP tools for Confluence-style page and attachment operations, tested page identifiers, and investigated whether attachment handling could cross the internal file-service boundary. The session also associated the challenge with the 2026 mcp-atlassian vulnerability family, but no accepted flag output survives.
escalation: The preserved plan aimed to place an SSH key through an attachment/file-write primitive, then read the user flag over SSH. Completion belongs to the team record, but the final commands are unavailable.
lessons: An MCP tool is an authenticated proxy into its backing application. Model the transport, tool arguments, URL construction, and the internal service separately. Do not present a CVE match as proof until the vulnerable data flow is demonstrated.
evidenceNote: Argentina was assigned to teammates. Ownership is credited to the team, while the missing final transcript is stated explicitly.

title: Signal starts here.
summary: A living record of machines, mistakes, attack paths, and the small observations that survive after the shell closes.
recon: This journal exists to make the work legible. Every entry starts with what was visible, what looked wrong, and which assumption was worth testing.
path: Full attack paths appear only when a target is retired or the material is safe to disclose. Active machines receive spoiler-safe field notes.
escalation: The point is not the flag. The useful part is the decision trail: why one route died, why another opened, and what should be remembered next time.
lessons: Write while the evidence is fresh. Separate observation from inference. Keep the commands that mattered. Remove secrets. Publish what teaches.
evidenceNote: This entry defines the archive policy used by the reconstructed writeups.
